newsitem.title: USA: Clinton must decide on out-of-court settlement.
newsitem.headline: Clinton must decide on out-of-court settlement.

text.p: Faced with the prospect of an embarrassing trial laced with lurid details, President Bill Clinton must decide whether to seek an out-of-court settlement in the sexual harassment lawsuit brought by Paula Jones.

In a stunning rebuke to Clinton, the nine Supreme Court justices ruled unanimously on Tuesday that Jones' lawsuit can move forward. They rejected Clinton's argument that sitting presidents should have immunity from civil lawsuits involving their personal conduct.

The court left the way open for Clinton's lawyers to use legal manoeuvres that could continue to delay the case. But legal experts predicted that even with delaying tactics the case will go to trial before Clinton leaves office in 2001.
So the conventional wisdom in Washington was that Clinton would direct his lawyers to seek an out-of-court settlement and try to avoid admitting guilt to Jones' harassment charges.

She says Clinton exposed himself and asked for sexual favours in a Little Rock, Arkansas, hotel room on May 8, 1991, while he was governor and she was a state employee. He has denied the charge and said he does not recall meeting Jones.

"If it goes through deposition to court, Clinton loses regardless of the verdict because all the lurid information becomes public and it reinforces some of the character baggage he has brought to the office," presidential expert Stephen Wayne said.

Jones' lawyers, enjoying a publicity bonanza because of the case, have made clear they are open to a settlement, saying the two sides attempted to reach one two years ago but could not agree on the language.
They said Clinton was willing to agree then to a statement saying, "While I don't recall Paula Jones, I don't deny her claim that she was in my room at the Excelsior Hotel."

Joseph Cammarata, one of Jones' lawyers, said she was willing two years ago to accept a statement that Clinton would read saying that he did recall meeting her, that she did nothing wrong and that he regretted some untrue assertions that were made about her character after she filed her suit.
Cammarata and his colleague on the case, Gilbert Davis, a Republican running for state attorney general of Virginia, told CNN it was up to Clinton's lawyers to make a settlement proposal now.
"I'm not going to propose something for them," he said. "It's up to them now to come to us with some kind of proposal."

Clinton's lawyer for this case, Robert Bennett, has appeared sceptical about a settlement, saying it will not happen if the deal involves Clinton paying Jones a lot of money or acknowledging something he believes was not true.
Bennett's next move was expected to be a motion seeking a dismissal of the lawsuit in the Arkansas federal court where the suit was filed.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, asked if the Supreme Court ruling set any sort of precedent, said: "It's the same precedent that was set in 1974 with Richard Nixon. No one in America is above the law, period."

"It's true over and over again, and it's the essence of the American system -- no one in America is above the law," he told reporters in his home state of Georgia. Asked if he believed activity from the case would threaten the smooth running of government, he responded: "Not at all."

Many legal experts were surprised not only that the Supreme Court ruled in Jones' favour but that the decision was unanimous, including two justices Clinton appointed, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer. In oral arguments earlier this year the justices had sounded divided on the issue.

"The court does try to act unanimously when it acts against the president of the United States but I didn't think they'd be able to do it in this case because they were so divided," Georgetown University law professor Susan Bloch said.
"I think it's in his interest to get a settlement. I think it would be in his interest to get this resolved and off the front page."

Clinton, in the Netherlands on a European trip, said on Wednesday he was concerned about the precedent for future presidents established by the court decision. He had argued that a president burdened with major responsibilities should not have to face such a trial while in office.

Clinton, whose re-election campaign last year made great use of public opinion polls, could only look with dismay at an ABC News "Nightline" poll that said six in 10 Americans agreed with the court that sitting presidents should not be exempt from private lawsuits.
